title: Life cycles, governance & limits of financial authority
blurb: Explain how linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles shape governance, and how limits of financial authority decide who can approve which spend.
question: A rail operator is upgrading a station (a linear build) and launching a ticketing app (built iteratively). The project manager may approve commitments up to a set limit. How should governance differ for the two parts, and what must the PM do when an unplanned cost goes beyond their financial authority?

teach.h: The life cycle shapes the governance
teach.body: A project's governance framework has to fit its life cycle. In a LINEAR life cycle, governance is built around formal decision gates at the end of each phase, with approvals and funding released phase by phase. In an ITERATIVE life cycle, governance is lighter but more frequent, working at release and time-box level, with the product owner taking many scope decisions inside tight, fixed time and cost limits. A HYBRID needs both, carefully aligned.

teach.caption: At each gate the sponsor and board re-check the business case and decide go, no-go or replan before releasing the next phase's funding.
Governance happens little and often. Most scope changes are absorbed by reprioritising the backlog, not by formal change control.

teach.body: A limit of financial authority is the maximum spend or financial commitment that a role may approve on its own. It covers committing money (signing a contract or order), not just paying invoices. Above the limit, the decision is escalated: project manager to sponsor, sponsor to board or portfolio. Limits keep large commitments at senior level, let small ones move quickly, make it clear who approved what, and protect the organisation from unauthorised spend.

head: Role
May approve up to
Above this
teach.caption: Real limits are set by each organisation's governance. The principle matters, not the numbers.
£60,000 is above the PM's limit, so the PM escalates with options and the sponsor decides.

teach.h: Scenario: Hartley Rail's station and app
teach.body: The station rebuild is linear: the board approves each phase at a gate and releases funding for the next. The ticketing app is iterative: every fortnight the product owner reviews the demo and reprioritises, and the sponsor joins a release review each quarter. Both report to one board so the app's launch lines up with the station opening. When ground surveys reveal £60,000 of extra drainage work, above the PM's £25,000 limit, the PM escalates to the sponsor with options.

teach.text: Two traps. First, iterative does NOT mean 'no governance': it means lighter, more frequent governance inside tighter time and cost limits. Second, having money left in the approved budget does NOT give the PM authority to commit it: a commitment above the PM's financial limit must still be escalated.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Linear: formal decision gates, phase-by-phase approval and funding.
Iterative: frequent, lighter reviews; product owner decisions; fixed time and cost.
Hybrid: both, aligned under one governance structure.
Define limits of financial authority and give the escalation route.
Explain why: control of money, speed for small decisions, clear accountability.
Linear governance: formal gates at phase ends; funding released phase by phase.
Iterative governance: lighter, more frequent, at release and time-box level.
Hybrid governance: gates and reviews joined up under one board.
Limit of financial authority: the most a role may approve or commit alone.
Above the limit, escalate: PM to sponsor to board or portfolio.

summary: You can now explain how linear, iterative and hybrid life cycles change a project's governance framework. You can also explain what limits of financial authority are, why they exist and how a commitment above a limit is escalated.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, where is the main governance control applied?
options: At daily stand-up meetings
At decision gates between phases
At each product owner backlog review
Only at the post-project review
A.why: Linear governance is built around formal decision gates at the end of each phase, where the business case is re-checked and the next phase is approved.

whyNot.0: Daily stand-ups are a team practice, mainly in iterative delivery.
whyNot.2: Backlog reviews by a product owner belong to iterative governance.
whyNot.3: A post-project review is for lessons; control must happen during the project.

A.q: What is meant by a 'limit of financial authority'?
options: The total budget for the whole project
The contingency held back for known risks
The amount a supplier may invoice monthly
The most one role may approve alone
A.why: A limit of financial authority is the maximum spend or commitment that a role can approve without escalating.

whyNot.0: The total budget is the approved cost; it is not the same as any one person's authority.
whyNot.1: Contingency is a reserve for risks, controlled through governance.
whyNot.2: Supplier invoicing is a contract matter, not internal authority.

A.q: Which BEST describes governance in an iterative life cycle?
options: Frequent, lighter reviews per release
No reviews until the final release
One formal gate at the end of each year
All scope changes go to the full board
A.why: Iterative governance is lighter but more frequent, working at release and time-box level, with the product owner deciding many scope questions.

whyNot.1: Iterative does not mean ungoverned; reviews happen throughout.
whyNot.2: Annual gates are far too infrequent for iterative delivery.
whyNot.3: Most scope changes are handled by the product owner reprioritising the backlog.

B.q: A project manager's financial authority is £20,000. She needs £35,000 of unplanned test equipment. What should happen?
options: She splits it into two £17,500 orders
She approves it as the budget allows
She escalates it to the sponsor
She asks the supplier to delay invoicing
B.why: The commitment exceeds her limit, so she escalates to the sponsor with the reasons and options.

whyNot.0: Splitting an order to dodge a limit defeats the control and is a serious governance breach.
whyNot.1: Available budget does not extend her personal authority.
whyNot.3: Delaying the invoice does not change the size of the commitment or who must approve it.

B.q: Why does a linear life cycle usually release funding phase by phase at gates?
options: To avoid having a business case at all
To commit step by step as risk reduces
To let the PM spend without any limits
To remove the need for a project sponsor
B.why: Releasing funding at each gate lets the organisation commit progressively, re-checking the business case as information improves and risk reduces.

whyNot.0: Gates exist to re-check the business case, not to avoid one.
whyNot.2: Gates strengthen control; they do not remove limits.
whyNot.3: The sponsor takes or recommends the gate decisions.

B.q: Which statement about governance on an iterative project is correct?
options: Scope is fixed and time and cost flex
The board must approve each new story
Formal gates replace all team reviews
Time and cost are fixed; scope flexes
B.why: Iterative governance sets tight, fixed time and cost limits per time box and release; scope flexes through backlog prioritisation.

whyNot.0: This describes the linear approach, where the scope baseline is fixed.
whyNot.1: Individual backlog items are prioritised by the product owner, not the board.
whyNot.2: Iterative governance relies on frequent reviews, not formal gates alone.

C.q: A hospital is building a new wing (linear) and developing a patient booking app (iterative) as one project. Which governance approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Gates for the build, reviews for the app
Phase gates only, applied to both parts
Time-box reviews only, across both parts
Two separate boards that never confer
C.why: A hybrid needs governance that fits each part (gates for the build, frequent reviews for the app) joined up under one structure so the parts stay aligned.

whyNot.1: Phase gates alone would slow the iterative app and lose its frequent feedback.
whyNot.2: Time-box reviews alone would not give the build its formal approval points.
whyNot.3: Unconnected boards risk the app and wing not lining up; hybrids must be aligned.

C.q: A PM with a £50,000 limit signs a £90,000 contract, arguing that the money is within the approved project budget. What is the BEST assessment?
options: Acceptable, as the budget covers it
Acceptable, if the PMO is informed
A breach: it exceeds his authority
A breach only if the cost overruns
C.why: Budget availability does not change personal authority. A commitment above the PM's limit must be escalated, whatever the budget says.

whyNot.0: Having budget left does not extend the PM's financial authority.
whyNot.1: Informing the PMO is not approval by the right authority.
whyNot.3: The breach is the unauthorised commitment itself, whether or not costs later overrun.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT a reason for setting limits of financial authority?
options: Keeping big commitments senior
Creating a clear audit trail
Letting small spends move fast
Removing the need for a budget
C.why: Limits of financial authority work alongside the budget; they never replace it.

whyNot.0: Keeping large commitments at senior level is a core reason for limits.
whyNot.1: Limits make it clear who approved what: an audit trail.
whyNot.2: Delegated limits let small decisions happen without waiting for seniors.

reteach.title: Organising a music festival
reteach.question: A festival has a stage built by contractors and a line-up that changes week by week. How should decisions be governed, and who can spend what?

blocks.body: The stage is built in fixed stages (design, sign-off, build, safety check), each signed off before the next: that is linear governance. The line-up is booked in weekly rounds, with the promoter swapping acts as availability changes: that is iterative governance. On spending, the site manager can buy kit up to £1,000, the festival director up to £20,000, and anything bigger goes to the investors.

blocks.caption: Each level decides within its limit; anything bigger goes up a level.

blocks.text: If the site manager splits a £3,000 generator hire into three £1,000 orders, the festival still has a £3,000 commitment nobody authorised. That is exactly what limits of financial authority are there to stop.

explain.body: Formal decision gates at the end of each phase. At each gate the sponsor and board re-check the business case, confirm readiness and decide go, no-go or replan, releasing funding for the next phase.

test.q: What typically happens at a decision gate in a linear life cycle?
options: The team plans the next time box
The product owner reorders the backlog
The business case is re-checked
The supplier submits its invoices
test.why: At a gate the business case, readiness and funding are re-confirmed before the next phase is approved.

whyNot.3: Invoicing is a commercial matter, not the purpose of a gate.

explain.body: Lighter and more frequent: reviews at time-box and release level, with the product owner deciding most scope priorities. Time and cost are fixed, so the limits are tight; scope flexes to fit them.

test.q: In iterative governance, who makes most day-to-day scope priority decisions?
options: The project sponsor
The product owner
The PMO manager
The full project board
test.why: The product owner prioritises the backlog, absorbing most scope changes between iterations.

whyNot.0: The sponsor owns the business case and fixed time and cost, not daily priorities.
whyNot.2: The PMO supports governance; it doesn't prioritise the backlog.
whyNot.3: The board is involved at release level and for changes to fixed time, cost or objectives.

explain.body: Each role has a maximum it may approve or commit alone. Above it the decision is escalated: project manager to sponsor, sponsor to board or portfolio. This keeps big commitments senior and small ones fast.

explain.caption: The escalation route for commitments above a limit.

test.q: What is the normal escalation route for a commitment above the project manager's financial authority?
options: PM to sponsor, then board
PM to team leader, then users
PM to supplier, then sponsor
PM to PMO, which then decides
test.why: Commitments above the PM's limit go to the sponsor, and above the sponsor's to the board or portfolio.

whyNot.1: Team leaders have lower authority than the PM, and users don't approve spend.
whyNot.2: Suppliers are outside the organisation's authority structure.
whyNot.3: The PMO supports governance but does not hold spending authority above the PM.

explain.body: A hybrid uses linear gates for some parts and iterative reviews for others. The governance of both must be joined up under one structure, with interfaces and dependencies managed, or the parts drift apart.

test.q: What is the MAIN governance challenge in a hybrid life cycle?
options: There is no business case to maintain
No financial limits can be applied
The product owner chairs the board
Aligning both parts' governance
test.why: Hybrid projects combine different control rhythms, so governance must be carefully aligned across the parts and their interfaces.

whyNot.0: A hybrid still needs a business case.
whyNot.2: The sponsor chairs the board; the product owner works in the iterative part.
